title.en: Double Integrals, Fubini's Theorem, Polar Coordinates & The Change-of-Variables Jacobian

body.en: While a single definite integral \( \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \) accumulates a function over a one-dimensional interval, a double integral \( \iint_D f(x, y)\,dA \) computes the continuous accumulation of a scalar field over a two-dimensional planar domain \( D \) — measuring volumes under surfaces, mass distributions with variable areal density, and probability densities. By virtue of Fubini's Theorem, 2D continuous integrals decompose into iterated single-variable integrations, while curvilinear transformations are governed by the Jacobian determinant.

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Definition 4.1: Double Riemann Sums & The Double Integral

body.en:
Let \( f \) be a continuous function on a closed rectangle \( R = [a, b] \times [c, d] \). Partition \( [a, b] \) into \( m \) subintervals of width \( \Delta x = (b - a)/m \) and \( [c, d] \) into \( n \) subintervals of width \( \Delta y = (d - c)/n \), forming \( mn \) rectangular sub-boxes \( R_{ij} \) each of area \( \Delta A = \Delta x \Delta y \). In each sub-rectangle, choose a sample point \( (x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \).

The double integral of \( f \) over \( R \) is the limit of the double Riemann sums as grid dimensions shrink to zero: \[ \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \lim_{m, n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n f(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A. \] When \( f(x, y) \ge 0 \), this limit represents the exact volume of the 3D solid bounded between the surface \( z = f(x, y) \) and the \( xy \)-plane over \( R \).

label.en: ▲ Level 1 Foundation — Theorem 4.1: Fubini's Theorem on Rectangles

body.en:
If \( f(x, y) \) is continuous on the rectangle \( R = [a, b] \times [c, d] \), then the double integral equals the iterated integrals in either order: \[ \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_a^b \left( \int_c^d f(x, y)\,dy \right) dx = \int_c^d \left( \int_a^b f(x, y)\,dx \right) dy. \]

Separable Integrand Case: If \( f(x, y) = g(x) h(y) \), the double integral splits into the direct product of two independent single-variable integrals: \[ \iint_R g(x) h(y)\,dA = \left( \int_a^b g(x)\,dx \right) \left( \int_c^d h(y)\,dy \right). \]

label.en: Proof of Fubini's Theorem for Separable Integrands

body.en: Let \( f(x, y) = g(x) h(y) \) on \( R = [a, b] \times [c, d] \). For any partition of \( R \) into sub-rectangles with sample points \( (x_i^*, y_j^*) \), the double Riemann sum factors algebraically by the distributive law of real numbers: \[ \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n f(x_i^*, y_j^*) \Delta x \Delta y = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n g(x_i^*) h(y_j^*) \Delta x \Delta y = \left( \sum_{i=1}^m g(x_i^*) \Delta x \right) \left( \sum_{j=1}^n h(y_j^*) \Delta y \right). \] As \( m, n \to \infty \), because \( g \) and \( h \) are continuous on compact intervals, both bracketed factors are standard single-variable Riemann sums that converge independently to \( \int_a^b g(x) dx \) and \( \int_c^d h(y) dy \). Because the limit of a product of convergent sequences is the product of their limits: \[ \iint_R g(x)h(y)\,dA = \lim_{m,n \to \infty} \left( \sum_{i=1}^m g(x_i^*) \Delta x \right) \left( \sum_{j=1}^n h(y_j^*) \Delta y \right) = \left( \int_a^b g(x)\,dx \right) \left( \int_c^d h(y)\,dy \right). \] Evaluating the iterated integral: \( \int_a^b \left[ \int_c^d g(x)h(y)\,dy \right] dx = \int_a^b g(x) \left[ \int_c^d h(y)\,dy \right] dx = \left( \int_c^d h(y)\,dy \right) \int_a^b g(x) dx \), identical to the product. Reversing the order yields the same result by symmetry. \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: ● Level 2 Analytical Application — Definition 4.2: General Regions & Order Reversal

body.en:
Double integrals extend to non-rectangular, bounded regions \( D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \):

  1. Type I (Vertically Simple): \( D = \{ (x, y) : a \le x \le b, \; g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x) \} \). The integral is evaluated by integrating \( y \) first: \[ \iint_D f(x, y)\,dA = \int_a^b \left( \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy \right) dx. \]
  2. Type II (Horizontally Simple): \( D = \{ (x, y) : c \le y \le d, \; h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y) \} \). The integral is evaluated by integrating \( x \) first: \[ \iint_D f(x, y)\,dA = \int_c^d \left( \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx \right) dy. \]
  3. Reversing the Order of Integration: If an inner anti-derivative is non-elementary (e.g. \( \int e^{x^2} dx \), \( \int \sin(y^2) dy \), \( \int \frac{\sin x}{x} dx \)), sketching the geometric boundary curves allows converting the region between Type I and Type II representations, making the integral elementary.

label.en: Worked Example 4.A (Level 2) — Reversing the Order of Integration

body.en:
Evaluate the integral by reversing the order of integration: \[ I = \int_0^1 \int_{3y}^3 e^{x^2} \, dx \, dy. \]

Step 1: Identify and sketch region \( D \):
The current iterated bounds are: \( 3y \le x \le 3 \) for \( 0 \le y \le 1 \).
This describes a triangle in the \( xy \)-plane bounded by the lines \( x = 3y \iff y = x/3 \), \( x = 3 \), and \( y = 0 \).

Step 2: Express \( D \) as a Type I region:
For each fixed \( x \in [0, 3] \), \( y \) ranges from the bottom boundary \( y = 0 \) up to the line \( y = x/3 \): \[ D = \left\{ (x, y) : 0 \le x \le 3, \; 0 \le y \le \frac{x}{3} \right\}. \]

Step 3: Evaluate the reversed iterated integral: \[ I = \int_0^3 \left( \int_0^{x/3} e^{x^2} \, dy \right) dx = \int_0^3 e^{x^2} \Big[ y \Big]_{y=0}^{y=x/3} dx = \int_0^3 \frac{x}{3} e^{x^2} \, dx. \] Substitute \( u = x^2 \implies du = 2x\,dx \iff x\,dx = du/2 \). When \( x = 0 \), \( u = 0 \); when \( x = 3 \), \( u = 9 \): \[ I = \frac{1}{3} \int_0^9 e^u \frac{du}{2} = \frac{1}{6} \Big[ e^u \Big]_0^9 = \mathbf{\frac{e^9 - 1}{6}}. \]

label.en: ● Level 3 University Rigor — Definition 4.3: Change of Variables & The Jacobian

body.en:
Let \( T: S \to D \) be a \( C^1 \) bijective coordinate transformation given by \( x = g(u, v) \), \( y = h(u, v) \) that maps a region \( S \) in the \( uv \)-plane onto \( D \) in the \( xy \)-plane.

The Jacobian determinant of the transformation is: \[ J(u, v) = \frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)} = \begin{vmatrix} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v} - \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}. \]

Geometric Derivation: A small coordinate rectangle in the \( uv \)-plane with sides \( \Delta u \mathbf{i} \) and \( \Delta v \mathbf{j} \) maps to a curvilinear parallelogram in the \( xy \)-plane spanned by tangent vectors: \[ \mathbf{a} \approx \left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}, \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}, 0 \right\rangle \Delta u, \qquad \mathbf{b} \approx \left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}, \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}, 0 \right\rangle \Delta v. \] The area of this mapped parallelogram is the magnitude of their cross product: \[ \Delta A = \|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\| = \left| \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v} - \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u} \right| \Delta u \Delta v = |J(u, v)| \Delta u \Delta v. \]

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem 4.2: Change of Variables Formula & Polar Coordinates

body.en:
Theorem: Under the smooth, invertible transformation \( T: S \to D \): \[ \iint_D f(x, y)\,dx\,dy = \iint_S f(g(u, v), h(u, v)) \left| \frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)} \right| du\,dv. \]

Polar Coordinates Transformation: Setting \( x = r\cos\theta \) and \( y = r\sin\theta \): \[ \frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(r, \theta)} = \begin{vmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{vmatrix} = r\cos^2\theta - (-r\sin^2\theta) = r(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = r. \] Since \( r \ge 0 \), the absolute value is \( |r| = r \), establishing the canonical area element: \[ dA = dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta. \]

label.en: Worked Example 4.B (Level 3) — The Gaussian Integral Proof via Polar Coordinates

body.en:
Prove rigorously that the Gaussian integral satisfies: \[ I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2} \, dx = \sqrt{\pi}. \]

Proof: The single-variable anti-derivative \( \int e^{-x^2} dx \) cannot be expressed in terms of elementary functions. However, write: \[ I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2} \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2} \, dy. \] Since the variables \( x \) and \( y \) are independent dummy integration variables, multiplying the two integrals yields a double integral over the entire plane \( \mathbb{R}^2 \) by Fubini's Theorem (Theorem 4.1): \[ I^2 = \left( \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx \right) \left( \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2}\,dy \right) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2+y^2)} \, dx \, dy. \]

Convert the double integral to polar coordinates where \( x^2 + y^2 = r^2 \), \( dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta \), \( 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi \), and \( 0 \le r < \infty \): \[ I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r \, dr \, d\theta = \left( \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta \right) \left( \int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2} \, dr \right). \] Compute the \( r \)-integral using substitution \( u = r^2 \implies du = 2r\,dr \): \[ \int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2} \, dr = \lim_{R \to \infty} \left[ -\frac{1}{2} e^{-r^2} \right]_0^R = -\frac{1}{2}(0 - 1) = \frac{1}{2}. \] Multiplying by the angular integral: \[ I^2 = (2\pi) \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = \pi. \] Taking the positive square root (since \( e^{-x^2} > 0 \)): \[ I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2} \, dx = \mathbf{\sqrt{\pi}}. \quad \blacksquare \]

caption.en: Region \( D \) between \( y = x^2 \) and \( y = 2x \). Integrating vertically (Type I) uses \( \int_0^2 \int_{x^2}^{2x} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx \). Integrating horizontally (Type II) uses \( \int_0^4 \int_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy \). Fubini's theorem guarantees both orders give identical results.

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps & University Pitfalls — Double Integrals

body.en:
• The Omitted Factor of \( r \) in Polar Coordinates: Writing \( dx\,dy = dr\,d\theta \) is the single most common error in integral calculus. Due to the area expansion of polar sectors, \( dA = r\,dr\,d\theta \). Neglecting \( r \) yields invalid dimensions and incorrect numerical integrals.
  • Variables in Outer Limits: In any iterated integral \( \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx \), the outer limits \( a \) and \( b \) must strictly be constants. An outer integral like \( \int_0^x \dots dx \) is mathematically meaningless and indicates a fundamental failure in reversing bounds.
  • Jacobian Absolute Value: In the change of variables formula, you must take the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant: \( |J(u, v)| \). If a coordinate transformation reverses orientation (producing \( J < 0 \)), omitting the absolute value yields an incorrect negative area element.
  • Separability Fallacy: You may only split \( \iint f(x, y) dA = \int g(x) dx \cdot \int h(y) dy \) if BOTH the integrand is separable (\( f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) \)) AND the region \( R \) is a Cartesian rectangle with constant limits! If the limits depend on \( x \) or \( y \), factoring across integrals is illegal.

label.en: Worked Example C — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 4 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 9 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (4)^2 + (9)^2 = 16 + 81 = \mathbf{97} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(4)(9) = \mathbf{18} \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 5 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 5 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (5)^2 + (5)^2 = 25 + 25 = \mathbf{50} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = \mathbf{12.5} \).

question.en: Evaluate the integral \( \int_0^1 \int_y^1 e^{x^2} \, dx \, dy \) by reversing the order of integration.

solution.en:
Step 1: Sketch and identify the region \( D \): The given bounds are \( y \le x \le 1 \) for \( 0 \le y \le 1 \). This is the triangle bounded by \( x = y \), \( x = 1 \), and \( y = 0 \).

Step 2: Reverse order to integrate with respect to \( y \) first: In the reversed order, \( 0 \le y \le x \) for \( 0 \le x \le 1 \): \[ \int_0^1 \int_0^x e^{x^2} \, dy \, dx. \]

Step 3: Evaluate inner integral: \[ \int_0^x e^{x^2}\,dy = \Big[ y e^{x^2} \Big]_{y=0}^{y=x} = x e^{x^2}. \]

Step 4: Evaluate outer integral using substitution \( u = x^2 \), \( du = 2x\,dx \): \[ \int_0^1 x e^{x^2}\,dx = \left[ \frac{1}{2}e^{x^2} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{2}(e^1 - e^0) = \mathbf{\frac{e - 1}{2}}. \]

question.en: Evaluate \( \iint_D (x^2 + y^2) \, dA \), where \( D \) is the upper half-disk defined by \( x^2 + y^2 \le 9 \) with \( y \ge 0 \).

solution.en:
Step 1: Convert region \( D \) to polar coordinates: The upper half-disk of radius 3 corresponds to \( 0 \le r \le 3 \) and \( 0 \le \theta \le \pi \).

Step 2: Convert integrand and area element: \[ x^2 + y^2 = r^2, \qquad dA = r\,dr\,d\theta. \]

Step 3: Set up and evaluate iterated integral: \[ \iint_D (x^2 + y^2)\,dA = \int_0^\pi \int_0^3 r^2 (r\,dr\,d\theta) = \int_0^\pi d\theta \cdot \int_0^3 r^3\,dr. \] \[ = \pi \cdot \left[ \frac{r^4}{4} \right]_0^3 = \pi \cdot \frac{81}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{81\pi}{4}}. \]

question.en: [Double Integrals, Fubini's Theorem, Polar Coordinates & The Change-of-Variables Jacobian · Practice 3] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 5t + 5 \), evaluate \( g(8) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 50 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 8 \): \( g(8) = 5(8) + 5 = \mathbf{45} \). Setting \( 5t + 5 = 50 \) gives \( 5t = 45 \implies t = \mathbf{9} \).

question.en: [Double Integrals, Fubini's Theorem, Polar Coordinates & The Change-of-Variables Jacobian · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
